note: A meta-review of roughly 110 studies on benchmark shortcomings, useful as a citable basis for discounting a headline score.
title: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation
explain_beginner: This paper reviews about 100 studies from the past decade that examine problems with AI benchmarks, which are standard tests used to compare AI systems. The authors group many concerns: test data can be biased or poorly documented, models may have already seen test material, and scores can confuse real ability with noise. They also warn that benchmarks often test only text models once, not how AI works with other data, people, or other systems. The review says benchmarks are shaped by commercial and competitive pressures, can be manipulated, and may not measure what matters. It matters because people, companies, and regulators should not trust a single score too much.
explain_business: For executives, this review warns against treating a single AI benchmark score as a reliable signal. The authors examined about 100 studies and found recurring problems: biased or poorly documented test data, test material leaking into training, noisy results, and tests that do not reflect real-world use. They also note that benchmarks can be manipulated and are influenced by commercial and competitive pressures that favor top scores over broader concerns. In practice, leaders should treat benchmark scores as one input, not proof, and ask how tests were built and whether they match the setting. It informs decisions about how much weight to give benchmark claims in oversight and regulation.
explain_practitioner: The authors conducted an interdisciplinary meta-review of roughly 100 studies from ten years that critique quantitative AI benchmarking. They synthesize problems including biased dataset creation, weak documentation, test material leaking into training, and difficulty separating meaningful signal from noise. They also connect these to broader concerns, such as overemphasis on single tests of text-only models while AI becomes multimodal and interacts with humans and technical systems. The review identifies systemic flaws: incentives pointing the wrong way, tests that may not measure the intended concept, unforeseen gaps, and manipulated results. Its key result is that benchmarking practices are shaped by cultural, commercial, and competitive forces, so scores deserve less automatic trust.
